notes: Assured tenancy possession appeal; Brooke LJ's section 9A analysis and refusal to suspend is clear.

enrichment.short_title: London & Quadrant v Root: refusal to suspend possession after partner's ASB
key_facts: Lorraine Root held an assured weekly tenancy at 53 Totlands Drive, Clacton; her partner Jay Barnes ran a car repair and scrap business from the property and intimidated neighbours and housing officers for about two years.
Possession was sought under Schedule 2 grounds 12 and 14 for breach of tenancy and nuisance; an interim anti-social behaviour order removed Barnes from the estate in May 2004.

Judge Yelton made an absolute 28-day possession order in September 2004, finding continued garden disrepair, refusal of access and breakdown of the landlord-tenant relationship despite Barnes' departure.
Root appealed on the basis that the ASBO made suspension of possession reasonable; Shelter acted for her.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against an absolute possession order made at a multi-track county court trial.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the judge was entitled to refuse to suspend possession having properly applied section 9A and balanced the tenant's hardship against the serious effect on neighbours.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 9A of the Housing Act 1988 a court deciding whether to make or suspend a possession order for nuisance must consider the effect on third parties; an ASBO against a household member does not automatically require suspension where the tenant's continued denial of breaches and refusal of access show the shadow of the past remains too heavy.
legal_issues: Whether the judge erred in refusing to suspend the possession order after Barnes left and an ASBO was in place
Whether section 9A required particular weight to be given to the effect of nuisance on neighbours
Whether the tenant's own breaches after Barnes' departure were relevant to suspension
linked_authorities: London Borough of Lambeth v Howard [1999] EWCA Civ 901

notes: Brussels II Article 11 lis pendens appeal; Thorpe LJ's preference for French characterisation is well reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Chorley v Chorley: Brussels II seisin and French divorce proceedings
key_facts: An English husband and French wife with four children married in 2000 after a French prenuptial contract choosing French jurisdiction; the husband issued fault divorce proceedings in Nice in January 2003 by Requête.
The wife later petitioned for divorce in London in January 2004; Wood J held the English court was first seised because the French Assignation post-dated her petition.
The Cour d'Appel d'Aix held the Requête commenced proceedings and that the French court was first seised by about twelve months.
The husband appealed, contending an English judge should not have determined the characterisation of French procedural steps.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Wood J's three-day hearing determining Brussels II lis pendens and first-seised questions in competing Anglo-French divorce proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Wood J wrongly exercised his discretion in determining French seisin locally rather than staying pending French determination, though the wife's London petition remained stayed.
enrichment.ratio: Questions of characterisation of a Member State's own divorce procedure under Article 11 of Brussels II should ordinarily be determined by that state's courts; Family Proceedings Rule 2.27A(2) does not oblige an English court to decide seisin when a stay pending foreign determination is appropriate, and filing a French Requête should be treated as the first manifest step initiating proceedings.
legal_issues: Whether the issue of the French Requête or Assignation seised the court for Article 11 purposes
Whether Wood J should have stayed English proceedings for French determination of seisin
Construction of FPR 2.27A(2) and its interaction with Article 11

notes: Mental Health Act section 11 practicability declaration; Bennett J's Article 8 analysis is thorough.

enrichment.short_title: R (E) v Bristol: practicability of consulting nearest relative under section 11
key_facts: The claimant suffered chronic mental health problems and had a severely strained relationship with her sister, who was her statutory nearest relative under the Mental Health Act 1983.

Her consultant psychiatrist considered consultation with the sister would damage her mental health; Bristol City Council accepted involvement of the nearest relative could be harmful but said section 11 obliged notification and consultation.
The sister indicated willingness to delegate nearest-relative functions to social services but the council maintained consultation remained practicable.
Judicial review was brought for declarations prohibiting notification or consultation without the claimant's consent.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review claim for declarations as to lawfulness of consulting the nearest relative under section 11(3) and (4) of the Mental Health Act 1983.
enrichment.outcome: Declaration granted that it was not practicable for the council to inform or consult the nearest relative under section 11(3) and (4); costs ordered against the defendant.
enrichment.ratio: 'Practicable' and 'reasonably practicable' in section 11 of the Mental Health Act 1983 may legitimately take account of consequences including the patient's wishes and health; where consultation would breach Article 8 and harm a competent patient, section 3 of the Human Rights Act 1998 permits a compatible construction relieving the approved social worker of the duty.
legal_issues: Whether section 11 required consultation with a nearest relative against the patient's wishes
Whether 'practicable' includes consideration of patient welfare and Article 8 rights
Whether section 29 provided an adequate alternative mechanism to remove an unsuitable nearest relative

enrichment.short_title: R (Conde) v Lambeth: section 17 support and EEA job seeker rights
key_facts: A Spanish national fled domestic violence with two young children and sought section 17 Children Act 1989 support from Lambeth after being refused homelessness assistance as not habitually resident.
Lambeth refused section 17 services, treating the children as not 'in need' and relying on Schedule 3 of the 2002 Act excluding EEA nationals from certain welfare powers.
The claimant argued refusal obstructed her rights as an EU work seeker and was discriminatory; she had been unable to find employment after over six months in the UK.
Lambeth's assessment contemplated section 20 accommodation for the children alone as a last resort and return to Spain.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Lambeth's refusal of section 17 support; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; Collins v Secretary of State for Work and Pensions did not entitle a work seeker to Children Act accommodation and there was no unlawful discrimination in suggesting return to Spain.
enrichment.ratio: Section 17 Children Act services are not social advantages facilitating access to employment for EU work seekers; Schedule 3 NIAA 2002 exclusion applies unless Community Treaty rights require support, and requiring a work seeker to return home rather than provide housing under section 17 is not disproportionate discrimination comparable with a UK national moving between regions.
legal_issues: Whether an EEA work seeker had Community law rights to section 17 accommodation
Whether Schedule 3 paragraph 3(b) disapplied the EEA exclusion
Whether refusal of support was discriminatory or disproportionate under EU law

enrichment.short_title: Verry v Furlong: adjudicator jurisdiction over extension of time response

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996

key_facts: Verry contracted to supply and erect cladding for Furlong; substantial delay led to competing final account and extension of time claims crystallising in August 2004.
Furlong referred a wide 'kitchen sink' final account dispute to adjudication, asking whether the extension to 2 February 2004 was correct or what the appropriate extension was.
Verry's response Section D detailed an extension to 27 July 2004; Furlong argued this was a new claim outside the crystallised dispute.
The adjudicator awarded Verry a longer extension; Furlong resisted enforcement on jurisdiction and natural justice grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 8 claim for a declaration that the adjudicator's decision was valid and binding pending final court determination.
enrichment.outcome: Declaration granted; the adjudicator had jurisdiction to consider Section D as part of the referred dispute and did not act unfairly.
enrichment.ratio: Where a referring party asks an adjudicator in unqualified terms to decide whether an extension of time 'is correct' or to decide the appropriate extension, the responding party may deploy its full defence including refined delay analysis; Section D was an enhancement of the July claim not a new dispute, and a responding party is not confined to earlier pleaded positions.
legal_issues: Whether Section D of Verry's response was a new extension of time claim outside the referred dispute
Whether the Notice of Adjudication limited jurisdiction to the 2 July 2004 claim
Whether the adjudicator acted unfairly in the time available

enrichment.short_title: Keane v Green: second appeal on shop counter conversion claim
key_facts: Mr Keane claimed in person that employees of the defendant stole three shop counters worth £3,000 in 1997 and obtained default judgment.
After the judgment was set aside, a district judge struck out the claim in July 2004, holding 'theft' was not a civil cause of action and the particulars lacked detail.
Keane had understood from the same judge in January that amendment was optional; he lost his temper and left the hearing.
By the appeal hearing amended particulars pleading bailment and conversion and a skeleton argument had been prepared, but Keane was absent and lacked a July transcript.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal (second appeal) against strike-out of a county court claim under CPR 52.13.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted; there was a compelling reason to hear the appeal given probable misunderstanding of the July hearing and available properly particularised claims.
enrichment.ratio: A second appeal may be permitted where there is a compelling reason even without a point of principle; a lay litigant alleging 'theft' may state a viable claim in conversion or bailment if properly particularised, and appellate intervention may be warranted where strike-out proceeded on a misunderstanding and adequate amended pleadings existed.
legal_issues: Whether CPR 52.13 compelling-reason threshold was met for a second appeal
Whether alleging theft without pleading conversion justified strike-out
Effect of amended particulars and skeleton argument not considered on appeal

enrichment.short_title: Hill v Clacton Family Trust: PTSD disability discrimination permission
key_facts: Miss Hill was summarily dismissed in February 2001 from work with young people; she claimed post-traumatic stress disorder arising from witnessing a fatal motorcycle stunt accident in August 2000.
The employment tribunal found PTSD could be a disability but held as a fact she was not suffering from it at dismissal; unfair dismissal was upheld separately.
On EAT review the tribunal emphasised she probably did not witness the incident as described, treating causation as relevant to whether she was affected.
DWP had granted disability living allowance on the basis of PTSD for the relevant period, creating inconsistent tribunal findings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal dismissal of a DDA 1995 claim.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted; possible misdirection on causation and failure to weigh DWP disability findings warranted full court consideration.
enrichment.ratio: Whether an employee was a disabled person at the material time is a question of psychiatric fact at dismissal, not primarily whether she literally witnessed the traumatic event as claimed; tribunals should not treat disbelief of the triggering incident as dispositive without addressing medical evidence, and inconsistent findings with other tribunals may indicate error of law.
legal_issues: Whether the tribunal erred by focusing on whether Hill witnessed the accident rather than whether she had PTSD
Whether failure to weigh DWP disability benefit findings was an error of law
Distinction between errors of fact and errors of law on disability status

enrichment.short_title: Montpeliers v Westminster: unlawful exclusion of barrier options from consultation
key_facts: Westminster made an experimental traffic order in 2002 installing barriers in Montpelier and Trevor Squares to stop rat-run traffic while permitting resident permit holders through.
RBKC objected to making the order permanent; the council excluded barrier-retention options from a September 2003 consultation after deciding in August 2003 to revoke the experimental order.
Residents had been promised full consultation including barrier retention at a December 2002 meeting before RBKC's formal objection.
A permanent 2004 order removing barriers and imposing a 7.5 tonne limit was later made and could not itself be challenged.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Two linked judicial review claims quashing August and December 2003 decisions on consultation and traffic scheme selection.
enrichment.outcome: Both decisions quashed; mandatory order requiring fresh public consultation including all barrier measures from the 2002 order; claimant's costs ordered subject to excluding expert report costs.
enrichment.ratio: Consultation must occur at a formative stage with an open mind on all materially relevant options; excluding barrier retention because of RBKC's objection was unfair, breached a legitimate expectation of full consultation, and vitiated the subsequent decision even though section 122 factors could be weighed without adopting that particular solution.
legal_issues: Whether barrier-retention options were unlawfully excluded from consultation
Whether RBKC's objection predetermined the outcome or evaded section 121B
Whether section 122 required consultation on barrier retention
Whether a legitimate expectation of full consultation was breached

notes: Occupiers liability hotel wall jump; Court of Appeal reversed breach finding applying Tomlinson principles.

enrichment.short_title: Clare v Perry: occupier's duty and deliberate jump from hotel wall
key_facts: Mrs Clare was injured at about 1 am on 29 March 1998 when she deliberately jumped from a 6–7 foot Devon stone wall beside the Widemouth Manor Hotel near Bude, having misjudged the drop in darkness.
She and companions had missed a courtesy bus and crossed from the car park to view the sea; her amputee partner had descended elsewhere over a lower wall.
The trial judge found breach of the common duty of care in failing to fence the high wall point and apportioned 50% contributory negligence.
A fenced beer garden was later erected on the bank but was not relied on as contemporaneous evidence of breach.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against liability judgment of HHJ Overend at Exeter Crown Court; damages assessment had been deferred.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; no breach of the Occupiers' Liability Act 1957 duty because fencing was not reasonably required against foolhardy deliberate departure by an unexpected route when adequate egress existed nearby.
enrichment.ratio: An occupier need not take steps to guard against deliberate risky conduct that is not reasonably foreseeable; the duty to prevent accidental falls is a different kind of risk from injury caused by a deliberate jump into darkness, and Tomlinson v Congleton confirms occupiers are not insurers against all visitor foolishness.
legal_issues: Whether failure to fence the wall breached the section 2 common duty of care
Whether risk of deliberate jump differed in kind from risk of accidental fall
Application of Tomlinson and Darby to change-of-level injuries
linked_authorities: Tomlinson v Congleton Borough Council [2004] 1 AC 46
Darby v National Trust [2001] EWCA Civ 189
Jolley v London Borough of Sutton [2000] 1 WLR 1082

enrichment.short_title: R v Cova Products: inconsistent Health and Safety Act verdicts quashed

statutes_considered.title: Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974

key_facts: Cova Products manufactured sheet vinyl using large calendar machinery with Banbury mixers; Carter Brothers were engaged to replace a mixer and hopper in October 2001.
After partial completion the conveyer was restarted intermittently while latch bolts remained to be tightened from an intermediate platform with gaps on both sides.
Carter's fitter Greenwood squeezed through a north-side platform gap alone, was caught by the moving conveyer and died; Cova's fitter Merilo had briefly left to fetch sealant.
Cova was convicted on counts alleging breach of duties to Greenwood under section 3 and to Merilo under section 2, but Carter was acquitted on the equivalent section 2 count.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction in the Crown Court at Newcastle upon Tyne on two Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 counts.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; convictions quashed as logically inconsistent with Carter's acquittal; costs from central funds.
enrichment.ratio: Verdicts under sections 2 and 3 of the 1974 Act in respect of the same fatal incident are logically inconsistent if the specialist contractor employer is acquitted but the host employer is convicted; the jury should have been directed that guilt on the Carter count was a prerequisite to conviction on the Cova counts, and once inconsistency is shown the burden lies on the Crown to prove safety of the remaining convictions.
legal_issues: Whether guilty verdicts against Cova were irreconcilable with Carter's acquittal
Proper order of counts and jury directions where section 40 reverse burden applied only to some defendants
Whether inconsistent verdicts were unsafe under Durante and Nelson principles
catchwords: Health and Safety at Work Act
linked_authorities: R v Nelson Group Services (Maintenance) Ltd [1999] 1 WLR 1526
Associated Octel Co Ltd v DPP [1996] 1 WLR 1543
